sections.html:
Northeast Arkansas holds Craighead County, crossed by Crowley's Ridge and run from two county seats: Jonesboro in the western district and Lake City in the eastern district. Jonesboro is the largest city. Other incorporated places include Bono, Black Oak, Caraway, Brookland, Monette, Bay, Egypt, Cash and Nettleton, which sits partly inside Jonesboro. The 2020 population was 111,231, and Arkansas State University is a major presence in the county.

A tax bill here depends on which city, school district and improvement district the parcel falls in, and not only on the county. Two houses with the same value can carry different bills.

sections.h2: Who sends the bill and who sets the value
sections.html:
Two offices do separate jobs. The Assessor decides what the property is worth. The Tax Collector sends the bill and takes the payment.

OfficeAddressPhone
Assessor511 S. Union St., Suite 130, Jonesboro870-933-4572
Tax Collector511 Union Street, Suite 107, Jonesboro; second office at 107 Cobean, Lake City870-933-4560

What the collector takes in goes to the County Treasurer at month's end, and the Treasurer hands it out. Schools get most of it. County offices, cities, fire and police pensions, libraries, roads, streets and improvement districts split the rest depending on where the parcel lies. Separately, the Assessor takes personal property reports, and the Circuit Clerk is where deeds and mortgages get recorded.

Start with the Assessor's appraised value and take 20 percent of it. Multiply that taxable value by the millage rate where the house sits. A mill is a tenth of a cent. Local voters approve the rate.

Whoever owns the property of record on January 1 is assessed, and billing lags a year, so each assessment turns into a bill the following year. A sale in mid-year leaves the prior year's bill open until someone pays it, which the title company normally handles at closing.

Appraisers come back to each property every 3, 4 or 5 years and weigh size, quality and condition of improvements against sales and rental data. Tell the Assessor when you add a room, build a garage or start renting out a house you lived in.

Payment window: first business day of March to October 15 of the year after the assessment. Past that, taxes are delinquent, Arkansas Code 26-35-501 adds a 10 percent penalty, and interest builds daily on delinquent real estate. Mail counts as on time with an October 15 postmark. The collector advises buying postage at the counter or requesting a hand postmark, since a machine stamp can be dated later.

  • The county runs a payment portal for paying online.
  • For delinquent personal property, the office takes cash, money order, cashier's check or card (fees apply) and no personal checks.
  • The collector must publish delinquent lists each year. The personal property list goes to a local newspaper before December 1.

Personal property tax is its own account, yet an unpaid one can snag a payment day. Learn what sits under your name before you book a closing.

Call the Assessor first. Wrong square footage or a bad property description often gets fixed with no hearing. For a true value dispute, book a hearing with the County Board of Equalization by the third Monday in August. The board listens to you and decides whether to change the number. The Assessor's office has the current schedule and forms.

A principal residence can earn the Amendment 79 homestead credit. Owners aged 65 or older, or totally disabled, can also ask for a freeze on taxable value. The credit was $600 at last report, and the legislature has considered raising it, so check with the Assessor before counting on a number.

sections.h2: Selling with taxes owed, step by step
sections.html:
Ask the Tax Collector for a payoff covering any older years too, and check for personal property tax under your name. The title company takes that total and pays the county out of what you would receive. Before closing, compare the legal description on the deed with the Assessor's parcel record so the recorded deed matches. After closing, give the collector your new mailing address so later notices reach you instead of the buyer.

Expect the title company to send you a payoff letter and a settlement statement that shows every charge. Read the statement before you sign. A cash buyer follows the same steps. With no lender involved, nothing waits on an appraisal, and the closing date depends on how fast the title work finishes.

Carry the deed, your newest tax statement, photo ID and receipts for any additions. Landlords should add the lease and rent records. If the house is inherited, add the death certificate and any court papers. Two offices are in Jonesboro and one in Lake City, so choose the one nearest your side of the county.

With seats in two towns, it pays to know where to go. The Tax Collector keeps a main office in Jonesboro and a second office in Lake City, and the Assessor is in Jonesboro. A seller on the eastern side of the county can often finish the tax part of a sale at the Lake City office and save a trip. Phone ahead to confirm hours and what each location can do, since not every service is offered in both places.

Title companies in the area deal with these offices daily, so a call from them for a payoff is routine. Tell them early which parcel and which owner name appear on the bill.

A long-unpaid bill can end in a land sale through the Arkansas Commissioner of State Lands, held as a regional auction covering Craighead and nearby counties. Opening bids equal the taxes, penalties and interest. You can redeem up to 4 p.m. on the last business day before the sale. Act 241, effective July 1, 2023, makes an auction sale final. Parcels that find no bidder go on an online list about 30 days afterward.

Selling first can stop the clock. A buyer who closes through a title company gets the bill paid from the proceeds, and nothing is left to certify.

The Circuit Clerk, who serves as county recorder, files the deed. Recording costs $15 for the first page and $5 for each page after, with a $300 cap on multi-instrument documents. The state adds a transfer tax of $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration on deals above $100, and the contract settles who pays.

  • Get a payoff or tax statement from the Tax Collector.
  • Check whether any personal property tax sits under the same owner name.
  • Confirm the deed's legal description against the Assessor's parcel record.
  • Ask the title company to pay the tax and record the deed the same day.

If the house has tenants, gather the lease and rent records before you list, since a buyer and the title company will ask for them.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in Craighead County?
faqs.a: The Craighead County Tax Collector, at 511 Union Street, Suite 107 in Jonesboro and 107 Cobean in Lake City. The phone number is 870-933-4560.

faqs.q: What is the property tax deadline in Craighead County?
faqs.a: October 15 each year. Later payments carry a 10 percent penalty plus daily interest on real estate.

faqs.q: How do I challenge my Craighead County assessment?
faqs.a: Contact the County Assessor first, then request a hearing before the County Board of Equalization. The last day to schedule one is the third Monday in August.

faqs.q: Does a mailed payment count if it is postmarked by October 15?
faqs.a: Yes. The collector cites Arkansas Code 26-35-501(c)(3)(A) and recommends getting a manual postmark at the counter to avoid delays.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Craighead County house that owes back taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The tax is paid from sale proceeds at closing. A tax-delinquent parcel can also be sold at a state auction, which is final, so settle the balance before the sale date if you want to keep the property.
